result:
A connection pool keeps a set of already-open database connections alive and lends them out: your code borrows one, runs its queries, and returns it instead of closing it, so the next request reuses the same connection.

It helps because opening a connection is expensive (TCP handshake, TLS, authentication, and on Postgres a whole new server process), often costing more than the query itself, and pooling pays that once rather than per request. It also caps the number of connections, so a traffic spike makes requests wait briefly for a free connection instead of overwhelming the database, which has a hard connection limit and uses memory for each one.

The main setting is pool size, and bigger is not better: a database can only do as much work at once as it has cores and disk for, so a pool of roughly 10 to 20 per app instance usually outperforms hundreds. Watch the total across all app instances against the database's limit; if you have many instances or serverless functions, put an external pooler like PgBouncer in front. The usual failure is a leak, where code never returns a connection (often a missed error path), and the pool runs dry and every request times out waiting.
